nodeData.note: Subjects, projects and the move to junior school.

children.note: Upper primary is the three years from Grade 4 to Grade 6. Children read and write more on their own, do practical projects, and learn about science, farming, their country and the arts. This is a draft for review — please check details with your school.

children.note: The middle part of primary school, after Grade 1–3 and before junior school.
Upper primary is three school years: Grade 4, Grade 5 and Grade 6.

manas.q: Which grades make up upper primary?

children.note: KICD's 2019 framework groups upper primary (Grade 4–6) and junior school (Grade 7–9) together as middle school.

manas.q: Upper primary and junior school together form which stage?

children.note: KICD pages we read do not give an age range for Grade 4–6. Children usually move up a grade each year after starting Grade 1 at about age 6.
Children now use the reading, writing and counting they learnt in lower primary to explore bigger topics.

Current KICD design pages list fewer learning areas than the 2019 plan. Home Science and Physical and Health Education are no longer listed on their own. Ask your school where those topics are now taught.

manas.q: Which two 2019 learning areas are no longer listed separately for Grade 4–6?

children.note: Learning areas are the subjects. KICD's Grade 4 and Grade 6 design pages list the same 15 headings, shown here in groups.
Reading, writing, speaking and listening in the languages used at school and at home.
Learners read stories, write short compositions and speak in class. At home: let your child read a label, a newspaper headline or a short story aloud to you.

manas.q: Name the two main school languages in Grade 4–6.

children.note: Learners build Kiswahili reading, writing and conversation. At home: chat in Kiswahili at supper, or ask your child to write the shopping list in Kiswahili.
Learners can study a local language of their community. At home: ask grandparents to tell a story or proverb in your home language and talk about its meaning.
KICD lists four foreign languages for Grade 4–6. Schools choose which, if any, they offer — ask your school.
Learners start with greetings, letters and simple sentences. At home: practise a few greetings together each day.

manas.q: Which four foreign languages does KICD list for Grade 4–6?

children.note: Learners begin with everyday words, numbers and short conversations. At home: label things in the house (la porte, la table) and say them aloud.
Learners learn basic words and phrases for daily life. At home: count to ten in German while setting the table.
Learners learn simple spoken phrases and a few characters. At home: let your child teach the family one new word a week.
Maths, science and agriculture — all with a strong focus on doing and trying things out.
Learners work with whole numbers, fractions, money, measurement and shapes. At home: at the market, ask how much change you should get, or measure flour for chapati.

manas.q: At home, what is a simple way to practise Grade 4–6 Mathematics?

children.note: Learners observe, test and make simple things — plants, water, the body, simple tools. At home: watch which wet cloth dries fastest — in the sun, shade or wind.

manas.q: What is the official name of the science learning area in Grade 4–6?

children.note: Learners grow crops, care for soil and learn about animals. At home: start a small kitchen garden or sack garden with sukuma wiki or spinach.

manas.q: Name one home activity that supports Agriculture.

children.note: Learning about society, the country and faith.
Learners study their community, county and Kenya: maps, resources, leaders and how people live together. At home: draw a map of the route to school together.
Christian Religious Education: Bible stories and how to live them out daily. At home: talk about a story and one way to show kindness this week.

manas.q: What do CRE, IRE and HRE stand for?

children.note: Islamic Religious Education: the Qur'an, the life of the Prophet and good conduct. At home: discuss a lesson learnt and how to practise it.
Hindu Religious Education: Hindu teachings, festivals and values. At home: share the meaning behind a family festival or prayer.
Learners draw, paint, make crafts, sing, play music and perform. At home: make a toy or musical shaker from bottle tops and a used bottle.

manas.q: Which learning area covers drawing, crafts and music in Grade 4–6?

children.note: Children learn best by trying things. Science and Technology and Agriculture are taught a lot through hands-on projects.
For example, testing which materials float or which soil holds water best. Children guess first, test, then explain what happened.
Learners make models and simple tools from things like cartons, bottles and sticks. Keep a box of clean recyclables at home.
Learners plant, water, weed and harvest, and keep simple records of growth. It links Agriculture, Science and Maths.

manas.q: Which two learning areas are most linked to practical projects like gardens?

children.note: Children write down what they did and saw: dates, measurements, drawings. This is how they show their learning.
Many tasks are group work: sharing jobs, listening and presenting together.
KICD's framework describes learning that serves the community, such as clean-ups. Ask your school how this happens in Grade 4–6.
Growing up as a good member of the family, community and Kenya.
Learners study the features, resources and people of their county and Kenya. Visiting a local market, river or hill helps.
Learners talk about rules at home and school, and how leaders are chosen and serve the community.
KICD's framework names children's rights as a topic woven across learning. Talk about rights together with responsibilities at home.
Planting trees, not littering and saving water are everyday citizenship.
Citizenship is one of the seven core competencies: being a responsible, caring member of society.

manas.q: Is Citizenship one of the CBC core competencies?

children.note: Creative Arts helps children express ideas, build confidence and use their hands.
Learners draw from life, mix colours and make crafts like weaving or modelling with clay.
Learners sing, keep a beat and may make simple instruments from local materials.
Learners act, recite and perform. Watching your child's class performance means a lot to them.
Physical and Health Education is no longer listed on its own for Grade 4–6. KICD pages do not show where it went, so ask your school how games and PE are taught.
Use bottle tops, old newspapers, sisal, clay and seeds. Teachers should not expect costly items — talk to them if a request is hard.
Using technology wisely and safely. It is one of the seven core competencies, practised across subjects.
Digital Literacy is a core competency, not one of the 15 learning area headings for Grade 4–6.

manas.q: Is Digital Literacy a learning area or a core competency in Grade 4–6?

children.note: Learners may use tablets, computers or phones at school to read, look things up or make simple projects. Ask what your school uses.
Teach your child never to share their name, school or photos with strangers online, and to tell you if something feels wrong.
Agree on when and how long devices are used. Keep screens out of bedrooms at night.
Digital skills also grow by talking about technology, using a radio or calculator, and learning with a phone when it is free.
CBC builds seven core competencies (skills) and values (good character) through every subject.
These are the skills KICD wants every learner to grow.
Speaking, listening, writing and working well with others — for example presenting a group project.

manas.q: Name the seven CBC core competencies.

children.note: Believing 'I can do it' and keeping going when work is hard.
Asking why, testing ideas and finding solutions, like fixing a leaking garden bottle.
Coming up with new ideas, stories, designs and ways of doing things.
Knowing how to study, find information and learn from mistakes.
The other two competencies, explained in their own branches of this map.
KICD's 2019 framework lists values such as responsibility, respect, honesty and care.
Doing your chores, caring for your books and finishing homework.

manas.q: Give two CBC values children can practise at home.

children.note: Greeting elders, listening without interrupting, valuing others' ideas.
Telling the truth and doing your own work.
Helping a younger sibling, a neighbour or a classmate who is struggling.
Teachers check learning all the time, not only in exams. National assessment details come from KNEC — check with your school.
Teachers watch, ask questions, check written work and give feedback. This is called formative assessment.

manas.q: What is everyday classroom checking called?

children.note: Learners do projects and tasks at school that count towards their record. Ask how your child's project work is marked.
Teachers may keep samples of your child's work to show growth over time.
Reports describe how well a learner meets expectations in each area. Ask the teacher to explain the levels used.
There is a national assessment at the end of Grade 6 — check the current name and timing with your school or KNEC.

manas.q: When is the upper primary national assessment?

children.note: If anything about assessment is unclear, speak to the class teacher. Steady daily learning matters more than cramming.
Small daily habits help children grow into independent learners.
A short, regular homework time in a quiet corner builds a habit.
Even 15 minutes of reading anything — stories, newspapers, labels — grows vocabulary.

manas.q: What daily habit most helps languages?

children.note: Work for a while, then stretch or get water. Tired minds learn less.
Ask your child to explain today's lesson to you or a sibling. Teaching shows what they really understood.
A bag check each evening: books, pencils, project materials ready for tomorrow.
Praise effort and trying again, not only correct answers.
Enough sleep and breakfast help children concentrate at school.
You do not need money or a degree to help — interest and time matter most.
'What did you learn today? What was hard?' Listen fully.

children.topic: Help with projects, don't do them
children.note: Guide, supply cheap materials and ask questions, but let your child do the work.
Shopping, cooking, farming and travel are full of maths, science and language.
Your skills — farming, trade, crafts, stories — are useful learning for your child.
Attend meetings, read notes and ask questions early when something is not clear.

manas.q: What should a parent do when unsure about a school task?

children.note: If your child often struggles to read or see the board, talk to the teacher; a check-up may help.
Notice and praise small improvements. Confidence fuels learning.
After Grade 6, learners move to junior school, Grades 7–9.
Junior school is the second half of middle school, for three years.

manas.q: Which grades come after upper primary?

children.note: KICD's Grade 7 page lists Integrated Science and Pre-Technical Studies, which are new after Grade 6.

manas.q: Name one learning area that starts in junior school.

children.note: English, Kiswahili, Mathematics, Social Studies, Agriculture, Creative Arts, religious education and languages carry on into Grade 7.
Ask your school how and where your child will join Grade 7, and what you need to do.
Let your child pack their own bag, manage time and do small tasks alone — skills they will need.
Moving up can be exciting and worrying. Listen to your child's feelings and reassure them.
